newsitem.title: UK: Labour would shape new UK regulatory landscape.
newsitem.headline: Labour would shape new UK regulatory landscape.

text.p: A few years ago the prospect of Britain's opposition Labour party ousting the ruling Conservatives would have sent icy shivers down the spines of many in Britain's City of London financial services industry.

But fears of more onerous regulation stifling London's pre-eminence as a world financial centre have been partly allayed by Labour's pre-election promises, and bankers seem to have taken the idea of a Labour government in their stride. If opinion polls prove to be right and Labour does win the election, which Prime Minister John Major on Monday set to take place on May 1, it will end 18 years of Conservative rule which has championed deregulation but led to what some see as an uncertain regulatory environment.

The head of a London-based fund management group told Reuters there was great concern in the industry over the confused regulation picture. He said he would be happy to see an incoming Labour government but believes the party has yet to clearly set out specific measures it would implement.
Despite these doubts, many in the City have been wooed by Labour and numerous bankers and senior company executives say they have had talks with key opposition figures.

But as the fund management head pointed out, whatever the political colour of Britain's ruling party, it would be highly constrained in terms of policy making by the growing power of the world's financial markets themselves.

Labour would legislate to end self-regulation of the industry by amending the Financial Services Act of 1986 to merge the array of Self Regulatory Organisations (SROs) with top financial watchdog the Securities and Investments Board (SIB).
At present the SIB supervises these "frontline regulators" which authorise firms to conduct investment business, monitor them, handle complaints and punish rule-breakers.

Labour argues self-regulation has not worked and has become too bureaucratic and expensive. Some in the City believe self-regulation has given way to a hybrid structure falling half-way between self-regulation and regulation by statute.
It says the failure of self-regulation is that it cannot serve two masters, the public and the trade interest.
If Labour does gain power, it would end the distinction between the SROs and the SIB, arguing that distinguishing between the two merely adds a layer of bureaucracy.

The SIB would become a statutory regulator answerable to the Treasury but operating at arm's length from it as a free-standing agency. Labour says this would simplify the structure, end regulatory arbitrage and clarify responsibility.

This would not only make the situation clearer for the general public, it would also give overseas investors and operators a clearer picture of the rules which applied to their particular area of investment. Labour said it would also end "confusion, duplication and bureaucracy" and cut costs.

Labour's shadow economic secretary Mike O'Brien envisages "a developmental process - reform rathern than revolution" to create a system flexible enough to adapt to market changes. But Britain will not have a version of the U.S Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) which would not be appropriate.
Labour intends altering the nature of regulation by trimming the number of rules whenever possible and is keen to consult with practioners before making any changes.

A senior investment banker told Reuters there was a fear, however, that the approach adopted by the Securities and Futures Authority (SFA), which regulates the so-called "wholesale" market, might be eroded under a new-look regulator. He pointed out the SFA "has a very active tradition of practitioner involvement in policy making" and that over a prolonged period its rulebook "has been rolled back", cutting down on the detailed regulation.
"We are strongly of the view that this is desirable in the wholesale market. If Labour's plans are carried though they should not imperil that aspect of the system.
"It is inappropriate to provide detailed customer protection information in a wholesale market," he said.

O'Brien acknowledges that the wholesale market needs to be addressed differently to the retail market -- those areas where private individuals are directly involved as customers. For the professionals there will be a "lighter (regulatory) touch based on the principle of "caveat emptor", or buyer beware.

One way in which Labour is likely to shape Britain's financial regulatory system over the next five years is if it has to select a new SIB chairman following the surprise announcement that Sir Andrew Large is to stand down in May.
Large's successor at the top watchdog will be chosen by the Chancellor of the Exchequer and the governor of the Bank of England.
O'Brien said Labour is not expressing a preference on who should succeed Large. "Labour will be considering this matter after the election and not before."
